facts.wett: WETT Inc. (Wood Energy Technology Transfer) describes itself as a non-profit training and education association that promotes the safe and effective use of wood-burning systems in Canada and acts as the national registrar of the WETT program. It says hiring a WETT-certified professional ensures wood-burning appliances are inspected, installed and maintained to current safety codes and standards, and helps homeowners meet insurance or regulatory requirements. Its site has a public directory of certified professionals. Office: 20 Richmond St. E., Suite 600, Toronto; 1-888-358-9388.
facts.nfc: NFC 2020 Article 2.6.1.4: every chimney, flue and flue pipe shall be inspected to identify any dangerous condition (a) at intervals not greater than 12 months, (b) at the time of addition of any appliance, and (c) after any chimney fire; cleaned as often as necessary to keep them free from dangerous accumulations of combustible deposits; and replaced or repaired to eliminate structural deficiency or decay and unsealed abandoned openings. Note A-2.6.1.4.(2): soot or creosote deposits more than 3 mm thick indicate the need for immediate cleaning, possible changes to burning procedures and more frequent inspections. Note A-2.6.1.4.(3)(a): structural deficiencies include a missing liner or inadequate supports or ties; decay includes cracking, settling, crumbling mortar, distortion, advanced corrosion, separated sections and loose or broken supports. Note A-2.6.1.4.(1): dense smoke at the chimney outlet indicates improper operation, incorrect chimney sizing or unsuitable fuel. Article 2.6.1.5: required clearances to combustible construction must be maintained, and combustible materials may not be kept within the clearance space.
facts.ofc: Ontario Fire Code Division B 2.6.1.4(1): every chimney, flue and flue pipe shall be inspected to identify any dangerous condition at intervals not greater than 12 months, at the time of addition of any appliance, and after any chimney fire; 2.6.1.5: cleaned as often as necessary to keep them free from accumulations of combustible deposits.
facts.b365: CSA B365-17 (8th edition, reaffirmed 2022) specifies requirements for the installation, alteration and maintenance of solid-fuel-burning appliances, including furnaces, boilers, stoves, ranges, space heaters, factory-built fireplaces and water heaters; it does not apply to site-built fireplaces, incinerators, process equipment or portable appliances. CSA's store shows a newer edition, B365:25.
facts.b415: CSA B415.1-10 (3rd edition, reaffirmed 2020) sets the test method for heat output, efficiency and emissions of stoves, inserts, factory-built fireplaces (burn rate under 5 kg/h), furnaces and hydronic heaters burning cordwood, chips or pellets; it doesn't cover coal.
facts.epa: US EPA: stoves certified to the 2015 standard were tested to a particulate limit of 4.5 g/h; the 2020 limit for new room heaters is 2.0 g/h tested with crib wood or 2.5 g/h with cord wood. EPA says certified stoves are cleaner burning and more energy efficient, and that fire officials recommend having the appliance, chimney and vent professionally inspected each year. Wood burns best below 20% moisture; test with a moisture meter. EPA stopped updating Burn Wise on October 30, 2025; the site is a historic record.
facts.apc: Québec APC FAQ: for occasional use, sweep once a year; for very frequent use, at least twice a year. APC member chimney sweeps can issue an electronic visual inspection attestation that insurance companies accept. Members hold the RBQ licence for the fuel (chimney sweeps 4.2, installers 10), pass APC training (70%), carry at least $2 million liability insurance and have at least 2 years in business. A certified stove carries a certification plate showing emissions, certification year and standards body, fitted only at original manufacture. The APC directory filters members by category, including inspectors (Inspecteurs) and chimney sweeps (Ramoneurs).
facts.bc: B.C.'s Solid Fuel Burning Domestic Appliance Regulation sets standards for wood stoves and other wood-burning appliances sold in B.C. The province says a modern, emissions-certified appliance reduces smoke but doesn't eliminate it, and that modern pellet stoves emit 80–90% less PM2.5 than most appliances burning regular firewood. The Community Wood Smoke Reduction Program offers incentives to replace old wood stoves with cleaner heating; exchanges to natural gas or propane appliances stopped being supported after January 1, 2023.

bcLocal.okanagan: The province's list of local programs includes the Central Okanagan Wood Stove Change Out (Kelowna and the Central Okanagan). We found no listing for the North Okanagan or Okanagan-Similkameen.
bcLocal.northern-bc: The province's list of local programs includes the Prince George Community Wood Smoke Reduction Program (Prince George and unincorporated areas of the Regional District of Fraser-Fort George) and programs in Mackenzie and Valemount. We found no listing for the Peace River Regional District.

facts.rebates: From the GSC research file (fetched 2026-10-08): NB Power's Total Home Energy Savings rebates for a wood stove ($200), wood or pellet insert ($200), pellet stove ($500) and wood or pellet boiler or furnace ($500) require the appliance to be US EPA or CSA B415.1 rated and WETT installed. PEI's biomass heating rebates require EPA-approved equipment or CSA-B415.1-10 (stove up to $1,000, or $1,800 for low-income households; boiler or furnace up to $2,000, or $3,500). Yukon pays 50% of costs up to $2,500 for an EPA-listed wood heating system with an approved final inspection report. The NWT's Arctic Energy Alliance rebates wood and pellet stoves at 50% of purchase cost up to $2,000 (2026/27).
